claims.text: Annealing Q235 steel at approximately 500 °C will produce a fine-grained state, whereas annealing it at approximately 800 °C will produce a coarse-grained state.
Increasing annealing temperature can increase grain size.
Coarser grains correspond to a lower grain-boundary density.
Lower grain-boundary density in coarse-grained Q235 promotes formation of a more uniform Fe-oxide scale during salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The oxide scale formed on coarse-grained Q235 will be more adherent and protective.
Fine-grained Q235 provides more grain-boundary sites for rapid oxide nucleation.
Grain boundaries act as fast-diffusion paths during high-temperature oxidation of Q235.
Rapid oxide formation associated with fine grains will be discontinuous rather than uniformly protective.
Discontinuities in the oxide scale allow salt penetration and accelerate corrosion.
Coarse-grained Q235 will form a more homogeneous and continuous oxide scale than fine-grained Q235 under identical high-temperature salt exposure.
Coarse-grained Q235 will exhibit less net mass change than fine-grained Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
Coarse-grained Q235 will corrode more slowly than fine-grained Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
Grain-size-dependent corrosion differences will be less pronounced at room temperature because kinetic processes are slower.
Unmodified Q235 is expected to show oxide characteristics and corrosion rates intermediate between those of the fine- and coarse-grained variants.
The proposed grain-boundary mechanism is primarily applicable in salt-rich environments at 700–900 °C, where oxidation is rapid and grain-boundary effects are pronounced.
At lower temperatures, or where inclusion chemistry dominates, grain size may not govern the corrosion response.
Annealing temperature may alter secondary microstructural features in addition to grain size, potentially confounding attribution to grain size alone.
The study will measure grain size, grain-boundary density, oxide-scale structure and phase, mass change, corrosion rate, and localized damage.
Failure of coarse-grained samples to outperform fine-grained samples in oxide integrity, mass change, or corrosion resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
